Ninth
nīnth
adj. & n. (next after the eighth; rendering Hebrew teshi'i, Greek enatos)
Saxon nigotha, from nine. In the Gospels the ninth hour is mid-afternoon — the hour of the evening sacrifice, of the loud cry, and of the temple prayer.

Biblical Definition

The ninth hour, about three in the afternoon, was the hour of the evening sacrifice in Israel, and the New Testament fastens three scenes to it. First, the death: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mat 27:46) — the true Lamb dying at the very hour the lamb was being bound on the altar in the courts a few hundred yards away. Second, the prayer of the church: “Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1) — and a man lame from birth walked. Third, the opening of the door to the Gentiles: “at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing” (Act 10:30), Cornelius at the hour of sacrifice, receiving the vision that brought Peter to his door. The ninth foundation of the city is a topaz (Rev 21:20). The ordinal thus gathers the whole gospel movement: the sacrifice offered, the church at prayer, and the nations brought in — all at the same appointed hour.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ninth as the ordinal of nine, the next after the eighth, and as one part of a thing divided into nine.

expand to see more

NINTH, a. The ordinal of nine; the next preceding the tenth.

2. Constituting or being one of nine equal parts.

NINTH, n. In music, an interval containing an octave and a tone.

Key Scripture

Mat 27:46 — "And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

Act 3:1 — "Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour."

Act 10:30 — "And Cornelius said, Four days ago I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,"

Rev 21:20 — "The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst."

Modern Corruption

The cry of the ninth hour is read as despair or as a mistaken Messiah; it is the opening line of Psalm 22, quoted from the cross, and it is the sound of penal substitution being paid.

expand to see more

Modern treatments of the ninth-hour cry usually take one of two exits. The first makes it a collapse of faith, a good man discovering at the end that no one was there. The second makes it merely a recitation, a dying man reaching for a familiar psalm with no real forsaking behind it. Scripture allows neither. It is genuinely the first line of Psalm 22 — a psalm that ends in worldwide worship, so it is not despair — and it is genuinely a forsaking, because He was made sin for us, and the Father turned from the sin He bore.

Held together, the hour preaches the doctrine. At the hour the evening lamb was slain, the Lamb of God was forsaken so that His people never would be. This is why Hebrews can promise, “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — the forsaking has already happened, once, to Another. Every believer who fears abandonment is being invited to look at three o'clock on that Friday and see the account settled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew teshi'i (H8671), ninth; Greek enatos (G1766), ninth — the hour of the evening sacrifice, the loud cry, and the temple prayer.

expand to see more

Hebrew teshi'i (H8671) — ninth; the ninth year and the ninth day of prophetic dating.

Greek enatos (G1766) — ninth; the ninth hour of Mat 27:46, Act 3:1, and Act 10:30.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth is about three in the afternoon — the hour of the evening oblation (compare Dan 9:21).

Usage

"“About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice” — the Lamb forsaken at the hour of sacrifice."

"“The hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” — the apostolic church kept the hour and a lame man walked."

"“At the ninth hour I prayed in my house” — Cornelius, and the door opened to the nations."
